sections.Business:
The company designs, makes, and sells a wide range of consumer technology products and related services. Its main product lines include smartphones, personal computers, tablets, and wearables such as smartwatches and wireless headphones. It also offers a spatial computer called Apple Vision Pro. On the services side, it runs advertising platforms, a device protection program called AppleCare, cloud storage, and several subscription offerings covering music, fitness, gaming, news, and video streaming. Payment tools include a co-branded credit card and a cashless payment service. The business is organized into five geographic segments — Americas, Europe, Greater China, Japan, and Rest of Asia Pacific — and sells to consumers, businesses, schools, and governments. In 2025, 40% of net sales came through direct channels like retail and online stores, while 60% came through indirect channels such as third-party carriers and resellers.

The markets the company operates in are intensely competitive. Rivals compete aggressively on price, copy product features, and in some cases sell products at little or no profit. The company holds a minority share in the global markets for smartphones, personal computers, tablets, and wearables. Some of those markets have experienced little or no growth. Competing successfully depends heavily on regularly introducing innovative new products and services, maintaining strong design and technology, and protecting intellectual property — though competitors frequently attempt to imitate both products and features.

Supplying the components needed to build its products presents ongoing risks. While many components are available from multiple suppliers, some come from a single or very limited source, and certain custom parts are unique to the company's products. Components across the industry are sometimes subject to shortages and significant price swings, and trade restrictions can raise costs or limit availability of materials including rare earths. The company has supply agreements in place but cannot guarantee it can renew them on favorable terms or secure adequate quantities if problems arise. To stay competitive, the company also invests continuously in research and development and holds a large global portfolio of patents, trademarks, copyrights, and other intellectual property rights, though no single right is solely responsible for protecting any one product or service.
sections.Risk Factors:
The business faces significant exposure to global economic conditions, given that the majority of its total net sales come from outside the United States and most of its manufacturing and supply chain operations are based internationally — primarily in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and Vietnam. Economic downturns, high unemployment, inflation, rising interest rates, and currency fluctuations can reduce consumer spending and demand for its products. These same conditions can destabilize suppliers, logistics providers, and other partners, leading to credit risks, liquidity problems, and disruptions across the supply chain.

Trade policy and geopolitical instability pose serious and immediate risks. Beginning in the second quarter of 2025, new tariffs were announced on U.S. imports from several countries including China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam, and the EU, with some countries responding with their own retaliatory measures. The U.S. Department of Commerce has also launched a Section 232 investigation into imports of semiconductors and related products. These measures can raise costs, limit product availability, force supplier changes, and require expensive operational restructuring — often with little or no advance notice. Beyond tariffs, the business is also vulnerable to natural disasters, climate-related extreme weather, industrial accidents, cyberattacks, and public health crises like pandemics, all of which can interrupt manufacturing, slow supply chains, and reduce consumer demand. Because many critical components come from single or limited sources, any disruption is especially difficult to absorb.

The markets for its products and services are intensely competitive and change rapidly, requiring continuous investment in new technology, hardware, software, and services. Success depends on consistently introducing innovative products ahead of or alongside competitors, as well as protecting intellectual property globally. Research and development investments may not deliver expected results, and regulatory actions or government investigations in various countries can force changes to or withdrawal of products and services from certain markets. Competitive pressure also drives down prices and gross margins, making it harder to sustain profitability while continuing to fund the innovation the business depends on.

sections.Cybersecurity:
Management takes full responsibility for identifying and handling cybersecurity risks, with the head of corporate information security leading the effort. That individual brings over 25 years of experience in the field, including leadership roles at other large technology companies, and has been running the company's information security team since 2016. A dedicated team of skilled professionals handles everything from writing security policies and training employees to monitoring threats, testing systems, and responding to incidents. A separate supplier trust team specifically manages the security risks that come through outside vendor relationships.

When security incidents occur, the company has a structured process to log, track, and escalate them to senior management and the board's audit and finance committee. The information security team also works with third parties when needed to help assess and test its security measures. Cybersecurity is formally included in the company's broader enterprise risk management program, which covers financial, operational, compliance, and reputational risks alongside digital threats.

The audit committee plays an active oversight role, regularly reviewing cybersecurity risks with management, including the general counsel and heads of compliance, business assurance, and internal audit. The committee receives updates on incidents as needed, and its chair reports key findings to the full board and recommends any actions deemed appropriate. Further details on specific cybersecurity-related risks are addressed separately in the risk factors section of the same filing.
sections.Properties:
The company's main headquarters is located in Cupertino, California. As of September 27, 2025, it owned or leased a range of properties across the United States and internationally, covering uses such as corporate operations, research and development, data centers, and retail locations.

These facilities serve all of the company's business segments rather than being dedicated to any single division. The company considers its existing buildings and equipment to be in good working condition and appropriate for carrying out its day-to-day operations.

No major property-related risks or changes were flagged in this section. The disclosure is largely routine, confirming that the company has the physical infrastructure it needs across multiple functions and geographies, without providing a detailed breakdown of specific locations, square footage, or associated costs.
sections.Legal Proceedings:
European regulators opened two separate investigations into the company's App Store practices under the Digital Markets Act. The first focused on how developers can communicate and promote offers to users outside the App Store; that investigation concluded on April 23, 2025, when the company was fined €500 million and ordered to remove restrictions that prevent developers from directing users to alternative purchasing channels. The company has appealed that decision. The second investigation, opened in June 2024, examines whether new contractual requirements imposed on third-party developers violate the same law. Preliminary findings were issued on April 23, 2025, and if a final violation is determined, the company could face fines of up to 10% of its annual worldwide net sales, plus additional fines for any failure to comply with a cease and desist order.

In the United States, the Department of Justice and several state attorneys general filed a civil antitrust lawsuit on March 21, 2024, accusing the company of monopolizing or attempting to monopolize the markets for "performance smartphones" and "smartphones." The DOJ is seeking equitable relief, and separate civil cases have been filed in state and federal courts seeking monetary damages. Separately, a long-running lawsuit brought by Epic Games resulted in a court finding the company in contempt of a 2021 injunction that required developers to be allowed to include links or buttons directing users to purchasing options outside the company's in-app payment system. On April 30, 2025, the court found the company in violation of that order, banned it from charging commissions on purchases made outside apps, and referred the matter to federal prosecutors to consider criminal contempt proceedings. The company has appealed to the Ninth Circuit, which agreed to hear the case on an expedited basis with oral arguments scheduled for October 2025.

Beyond these major cases, the company faces a range of other legal proceedings arising from ordinary business operations. Some matters were settled during the fourth quarter of 2025 without a material impact on its finances. However, the company acknowledges that legal outcomes are unpredictable, and if one or more cases were resolved against it for amounts exceeding management's expectations, the financial impact on the company in that period could be significant.

sections.Management\u2019s Discussion and Analysi:
Total net sales grew 6% to $416.161 billion in fiscal 2025, up from $391.035 billion in 2024. Growth was broad-based across most regions and product categories. The Americas rose 7% to $178.353 billion, Europe grew 10% to $111.032 billion, Japan climbed 15% to $28.703 billion, and Rest of Asia Pacific increased 10% to $33.696 billion. The one exception was Greater China, which fell 4% to $64.377 billion, dragged down by weaker iPhone sales. By product, Services was the standout, jumping 14% to $109.158 billion, while iPhone grew 4% to $209.586 billion, Mac rose 12% to $33.708 billion, and iPad gained 5% to $28.023 billion. Wearables, Home and Accessories was the only category to decline, falling 4% to $35.686 billion. The overall gross margin percentage improved to 46.9% from 46.2%, with Services gross margin reaching 75.4%, up from 73.9%. Products gross margin percentage slipped slightly from 37.2% to 36.8%, partly because of tariff costs. Operating expenses rose 8% to $62.151 billion, with research and development spending up 10% to $34.550 billion, driven largely by higher headcount and infrastructure costs.

Starting in the second quarter of 2025, the U.S. announced new tariffs on imports from multiple countries including China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam, and the EU. Several of those countries responded with or threatened their own retaliatory tariffs. The situation remains fluid, with further changes possible, including potential sector-specific tariffs on semiconductors and related products. These measures have already begun affecting product gross margins and could further impact the supply chain, availability of raw materials, pricing, and overall consumer sentiment. The company has flagged this as a significant and ongoing uncertainty that may materially affect future financial results.

The company ended fiscal 2025 with $132.4 billion in cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities, which it considers sufficient to cover its needs over the next 12 months and beyond. Outstanding fixed-rate debt totaled $91.3 billion in principal, with $12.4 billion due within 12 months and $37.0 billion in future interest payments. The company also had $8.0 billion in short-term commercial paper outstanding. Other near-term obligations include $2.6 billion in lease payments due within 12 months on $16.8 billion in total fixed lease commitments, and $55.4 billion of the $56.2 billion in manufacturing purchase obligations payable within the next year, reflecting the company's heavy reliance on outsourced manufacturing partners and component suppliers.
sections.Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures:
The company faces financial risk from two main sources: changing interest rates and shifting foreign currency exchange rates. On the interest rate side, higher rates would hurt the value of its investment portfolio and raise borrowing costs on its term debt. A hypothetical 1 percentage point rise in interest rates would have reduced the fair value of its investment portfolio by $2,416 million in 2025 (compared to $2,755 million in 2024), and would have increased annual interest expense on its term debt by $129 million in 2025 (compared to $139 million in 2024). To manage this risk, the company may use financial hedging tools, match interest-rate-sensitive assets against liabilities, or control how long its investments and debts run.

The company also earns a significant portion of its revenue in currencies other than the U.S. dollar, which exposes it to foreign exchange risk. When the U.S. dollar strengthens, the company's sales and profit margins, when converted back to dollars, decline in value. Exchange rate swings can also affect the value of certain assets and liabilities on its balance sheet. To limit this exposure, the company may use derivative contracts, offset currency positions, or adjust the local prices of its products and services in affected markets.

To estimate how much it could lose on a single bad day in foreign currency derivative positions, the company used a statistical model called Value-at-Risk, run with a Monte Carlo simulation. With 95% confidence, it estimated a maximum one-day loss in fair value of $590 million as of its most recent fiscal year-end, up from $538 million the prior year. The company notes that while it hedges many of its currency exposures, it sometimes chooses not to hedge certain positions due to cost or accounting considerations — though changes in its underlying currency exposures generally offset shifts in the value of its hedging instruments.
sections.Financial Statements and Supplementary D:
Total revenue grew to $416,161 million in fiscal year 2025, up from $391,035 million the prior year and $383,285 million two years earlier. Products brought in $307,003 million while Services contributed $109,158 million, continuing a trend of strong services growth. Net income rose sharply to $112,010 million, compared to $93,736 million in 2024 and $96,995 million in 2023, with diluted earnings per share of $7.46. The tax bill dropped significantly to $20,719 million from $29,749 million the year before, which contributed meaningfully to the profit increase. Operating income reached $133,050 million, and total operating expenses were $62,151 million, with research and development spending climbing to $34,550 million.

On the balance sheet, total assets stood at $359,241 million, down slightly from $364,980 million the prior year. Cash and cash equivalents rose to $35,934 million from $29,943 million, while marketable securities declined both in current and non-current categories. Total liabilities fell notably from $308,030 million to $285,508 million, driven by reductions in term debt and other liabilities. Shareholders' equity improved to $73,733 million from $56,950 million, even as the company spent $90,052 million repurchasing its own stock and paid $15,413 million in dividends, declaring $1.02 per share.

Cash generated from operations came in at $111,482 million, slightly below the prior year's $118,254 million. Investing activities generated $15,195 million, largely from proceeds on maturing and sold securities. Financing activities used $120,686 million, dominated by the $90,711 million in stock buybacks and $15,421 million in dividend payments. Cash paid for income taxes jumped to $43,369 million from $26,102 million the year before, a significant increase worth noting. The share count continued to shrink, with basic shares falling from roughly 15.3 billion to 14.9 billion, reflecting the ongoing buyback program.

sections.Controls and Procedures:
The company's top executives — its principal executive officer and principal financial officer — concluded that the company's disclosure controls and procedures were effective as of September 27, 2025. This means they are satisfied that important financial and operational information is being properly recorded, reported on time, and shared with the right people internally so that timely decisions can be made. Management also assessed the company's internal control over financial reporting using a widely recognized standard — the 2013 Internal Control – Integrated Framework — and concluded that those controls were also effective as of the same date. Ernst & Young LLP, the company's independent auditing firm, reviewed and issued its own report on those internal controls.

Management is transparent about the fact that no system of internal controls can guarantee perfect results. Even a well-designed system can only provide reasonable, not absolute, assurance against errors or fraud. Controls cost money and require resources, and their effectiveness can weaken over time as business conditions change or as compliance with internal policies slips. These are acknowledged limitations built into any control system, not unique problems specific to this company.

Finally, there were no changes to internal controls during the fourth quarter of 2025 that materially affected — or were likely to materially affect — the reliability of the company's financial reporting. This means the systems and processes in place remained stable through the end of the fiscal year, with no significant overhauls or breakdowns identified during that period.

sections.Disclosure Regarding Foreign Jurisdictio:
Not applicable sections of regulatory filings typically contain no substantive information to summarize. This particular item requires companies to disclose whether they operate in foreign jurisdictions that block oversight bodies from inspecting their auditors — a concern primarily relevant to companies with significant operations in certain countries where regulators restrict outside audit reviews.

Since the company indicated this item does not apply, it is not subject to these restrictions. This means its auditing firm can be fully inspected by the relevant regulatory bodies without interference from any foreign government, which is generally a positive sign for transparency and investor confidence.

No financial figures, risks, or operational details are associated with this disclosure. The single relevant fact is simply that the company has no foreign jurisdiction complications of this kind, and no further action or concern is raised by this portion of the filing.
sections.Directors, Executive Officers and Corpor:
The company has chosen not to include details about its directors, executive officers, or corporate governance practices directly in this filing. Instead, that information will appear in a separate document — a definitive proxy statement — which will be submitted to the SEC within 120 days after September 27, 2025. This proxy statement is being prepared in connection with the company's 2026 annual shareholder meeting.

By referencing the proxy statement rather than restating its contents, the company is using a standard but legally permitted approach to fulfill this disclosure requirement. The actual details — such as who sits on the board, who leads the company, and how governance is structured — will only become available once that proxy statement is filed and made public.

For anyone trying to evaluate the company's leadership or governance practices, this section provides no substantive information on its own. Readers would need to locate and review the 2026 proxy statement separately to find the relevant details about directors and executives.

sections.Exhibit and Financial Statement Schedule:
This section lists all the financial statements included in the annual report, covering three fiscal years ending September 27, 2025, September 28, 2024, and September 30, 2023. The statements include income statements, balance sheets, cash flow statements, and equity statements, along with accompanying notes. The independent auditor is Ernst & Young LLP, identified by PCAOB firm ID number 00042. All supplemental financial schedules have been left out because either the information is not relevant or it is already covered within the main financial statements.

The section also catalogs a long list of exhibits filed with or incorporated by reference into the report. These include the company's founding and governance documents, such as its restated articles of incorporation filed August 3, 2020, and amended bylaws effective August 20, 2024. A large portion of the exhibits covers debt instruments — specifically, dozens of officer's certificates dating back to 2013 that set the terms for various notes issued to investors, with interest rates ranging from 0.000% to 4.850% and maturities spread across many years. The most recent debt issuance listed is from May 12, 2025, covering four sets of notes with rates of 4.000%, 4.200%, 4.500%, and 4.750%, due between 2028 and 2035.

Several exhibits relate to employee and executive compensation arrangements, marked with an asterisk to flag them as management contracts or compensatory plans. These include the employee stock purchase plan amended November 6, 2024, the 2022 employee stock plan, various forms of restricted stock unit and performance award agreements for both general employees and the CEO, and an executive cash incentive plan. An insider trading policy is also listed as a previously filed exhibit. Certain documents defining the rights of long-term debt holders were omitted from the filing but the company committed to provide them to the SEC upon request.
